newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgaria finds CD piracy fight tough going.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgaria finds CD piracy fight tough going.

text.p: Bulgaria, under pressure to clamp down on mass production of pirated compact discs, brought its first case to court this month but the defendant was acquitted for lack of evidence.

The case in the town of Veliko Tarnovo underlined difficulties faced by the authorities battling a trade which has blossomed since the end of one-party rule, taking advantage of Bulgaria's sophisticated technology and inadequate legal controls.
A regional court on June 11 rejected the case against Marko Mihailov, the 37-year-old manager of local firm SMC, who was charged with producing CDs in 1995-96 in breach of Bulgarian copyright law.

Stanislava Armoutlieva, representative of the Dutch company PolyGram NV and its licensee Virginia Records, said there had been "some serious gaps in the materials presented to the court" but described the case as a positive signal.
Audio and video piracy has boomed with the liberalisation of trade since the fall of the communist government in 1989.

The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) has estimated illegal production in Bulgaria at 15 million compact discs a year, costing the European recording industry some $100 million.
SIZE OF THE ILLEGAL CD MARKET

The worldwide body, which groups industry giants like PolyGram, BMG and EMI, has urged Bulgaria to act against five CD plants which are estimated to supply one in eight of all illegal copies on the world's CD black market.

The IFPI estimates high quality Bulgarian pirate CDs are flowing into Russia alone at a rate of one million a month. From there they are distributed to the Baltic states, Finland, Scandinavia and on to the world market.

Bulgaria's foreign ministry last month invited reporters and European Union ambassadors to the DZU plant in the central town of Stara Zagora to see the legitimate CD production industry at work. Only three diplomats turned up.

The European Union's External Relations commissioner Hans van den Broek, who visited Sofia in March, urged the government to take tougher measures for protecting intellectual property rights in view of Bulgaria's commitments as a member of the World Trade Organisation.
A week later Bulgarian police launched a crackdown on firms suspected of making illegal CDs.
In one case reported by the IFPI, a raid of the Sofia to Moscow train revealed three carriages packed with 50,000 compact discs hidden behind seats and under panels on the floor.
"Train conductors, as well as the criminals disguised as tourists, had the CDs in their luggage," an IFPI report said.

Dimitar Enchev, director of the National Centre for Copyright Protection (NCCP) at the Ministry of Culture said that in the last six months police had investigated more than 280 producers and vendors of compact discs.
MEASURES TAKEN

The threat of raids has driven vendors away from the market stalls in Sofia's central Slaveikov Square, but the crackdown on retailers does not reach the highly-organised groups at the heart of the trade.

The new cabinet which took office in May is expected to establish a commission on copyright control involving seven ministries, police and legal authorities, Enchev said. The comission will coordinate action against copyright abuse.
Manufacturers must register orders with the NCCP to make sure they are legitimate. A system of identification codes engraved on CDs to identify the producer has been introduced.

But Bulgaria, which is second only to China in the export of pirated CDs, has not so far fully implemented its anti-piracy regulations, officials say. Washington put Bulgaria on a "watch list" last October.
The IFPI opened an office in Sofia this year but has not attemped legal action against producers or distributors.
Officials said they were waiting for "a very clear case" and the right timing, realising that the plants were run by powerful organisations.
